title: Πουλυδάμαντος βουλή
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Paris, angered at the death of his guest-friend Harpalion, shoots Euchenor of Corinth, a rich man who had boarded ship knowing from his father, the seer Polyidus, that he must die either of sickness at home or at the hands of the Trojans. Hector, who does not know that the Argives are cutting his men down on the left, presses on where the wall is lowest, and the Boeotians, Athenians, Epeans and Phthians hold him off the ships. Ajax son of Oileus fights close beside Telamonian Ajax like two oxen under one yoke, while the Locrians shoot from behind with bows and slings. Polydamas then tells Hector to fall back and call the chiefs to council, warning that a man who never has enough of war is waiting at the ships.

sentences.t: τοῦ δὲ Πάρις μάλα θυμὸν ἀποκταμένοιο χολώθη·
sentences.tr: tou de Paris mala thymon apoktamenoio cholōthē·
sentences.l: And over him, killed, Paris was greatly angered in heart;
sentences.i: And Paris was deeply angered in his heart at the man’s death;
sentences.n: τοῦ is the man killed at the end of the last part, Harpalion, and the genitive τοῦ … ἀποκταμένοιο (‘him having been killed’) gives the cause of Paris’ anger. ἀποκταμένοιο is the short epic aorist participle of ἀποκτείνω (stem κτα-, passive in sense) with the epic genitive ending -οιο. θυμόν is an accusative of respect: angered ‘in the heart’. χολώθη is from χολόω, ‘anger’, which belongs with χόλος ‘anger’; the next line uses a different verb, χώομαι ‘be incensed’.

sentences.t: ξεῖνος γάρ οἱ ἔην πολέσιν μετὰ Παφλαγόνεσσι·
sentences.tr: xeinos gar hoi eēn polesin meta Paphlagonessi·
sentences.l: for a guest-friend to him he was among the many Paphlagonians;
sentences.i: for the man was Paris’ guest-friend among the many Paphlagonians;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος names the bond of hospitality between two men of different peoples, and the house rendering ‘guest-friend’ is used wherever that bond is meant; it is why a stranger’s death touches Paris. οἱ ‘to him’ is Paris. ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν), πολέσιν the epic dative plural of πολύς, and Παφλαγόνεσσι has the epic dative plural -εσσι. The Paphlagonians are Harpalion’s people, who carried him off at the end of the last part.

sentences.t: τοῦ ὅ γε χωόμενος προΐει χαλκήρε’ ὀϊστόν.
sentences.tr: tou ho ge chōomenos proïei chalkēre’ oïston.
sentences.l: For his sake he, being incensed, sent forth a bronze-fitted arrow.
sentences.i: Incensed on his account, Paris sent forth a bronze-fitted arrow.
sentences.n: τοῦ points back to the dead man, as in line 660, and again gives the reason; ὅ γε ‘he’ is Paris, since in Homer forms like ὅ are often pronouns. χωόμενος is from χώομαι ‘be incensed’, the verb kept apart from χολόω ‘anger’ in 660. προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. χαλκήρε’ is χαλκήρεα, the masculine accusative of χαλκήρης ‘fitted with bronze’, with its uncontracted ending elided before ὀϊστόν. The target is named in the next sentence.

sentences.t:
ἦν δέ τις Εὐχήνωρ Πολυΐδου μάντιος υἱὸς
ἀφνειός τ’ ἀγαθός τε Κορινθόθι οἰκία ναίων,
ὅς ῥ’ εὖ εἰδὼς κῆρ’ ὀλοὴν ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβαινε·
sentences.tr:
ēn de tis Euchēnōr Polyïdou mantios huios
aphneios t’ agathos te Korinthothi oikia naiōn,
hos rh’ eu eidōs kēr’ oloēn epi nēos ebaine·
sentences.i: There was a certain Euchenor, son of Polyidus the seer, a rich and good man with his home at Corinth, who went aboard a ship knowing well the deadly spirit of death;
sentences.n: ἦν δέ τις ‘and there was a certain’ is how Homer brings in a man who has not been mentioned before; he is about to be hit. Πολυΐδου is the genitive of Πολύϊδος (spelled that way at 666), a seer. Κορινθόθι has the suffix -θι ‘at’: his home is ‘at Corinth’. ὅς ῥ’ (= ὅς ῥα) is a relative, and the γάρ of the next line explains how he knew. κῆρ’ is κῆρα, a death-fate (κήρ, the power that brings a man’s death), not κῆρ ‘heart’. ἔβαινε is the imperfect of βαίνω; with ἐπί and the genitive νηός it is ‘went on board’.

sentences.t:
πολλάκι γάρ οἱ ἔειπε γέρων ἀγαθὸς Πολύϊδος
νούσῳ ὑπ’ ἀργαλέῃ φθίσθαι οἷς ἐν μεγάροισιν,
ἢ μετ’ Ἀχαιῶν νηυσὶν ὑπὸ Τρώεσσι δαμῆναι·
sentences.tr:
pollaki gar hoi eeipe gerōn agathos Polyïdos
nousōi hyp’ argaleēi phthisthai hois en megaroisin,
ē met’ Achaiōn nēusin hypo Trōessi damēnai·
sentences.i: for the good old man Polyidus had often told him that he would perish of a grievous sickness in his own halls, or be overcome by the Trojans among the Achaeans’ ships;
sentences.n: The seer’s warning is reported with infinitives: ἔειπε (the epic aorist of εἶπον ‘say’, here ‘told’) takes φθίσθαι ‘to perish’ and δαμῆναι ‘to be subdued’, so there are two ways to die, ‘either … or’, although only the second is marked with ἤ. νούσῳ is the epic νοῦσος ‘sickness’, and ὑπ’ ἀργαλέῃ stands between it and its adjective. οἷς is the possessive ‘his own’, not a relative, and μεγάροισιν the epic dative plural. πολλάκι is the epic πολλάκις ‘often’.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥ’ ἅμα τ’ ἀργαλέην θωὴν ἀλέεινεν Ἀχαιῶν
νοῦσόν τε στυγερήν, ἵνα μὴ πάθοι ἄλγεα θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
tō rh’ hama t’ argaleēn thōēn aleeinen Achaiōn
nouson te stygerēn, hina mē pathoi algea thymōi.
sentences.l:
therefore both a grievous penalty of the Achaeans he avoided
and a hateful sickness, so that he might not suffer pains in his heart.
sentences.i: That is why he shunned both the Achaeans’ grievous penalty and the hateful sickness, so as not to suffer pains in his heart.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore’ (= τῷ), and ἅμα τε … τε works like ‘both … and’. θωή is ‘penalty, fine’; the line does not say what the penalty was or who would exact it. ἀλέεινεν is the imperfect of ἀλεείνω ‘shun’, without augment. ἵνα μή with the optative πάθοι is a purpose clause, ‘so that he might not suffer’; ἄλγεα are ‘pains’, θυμῷ ‘in his heart’.

sentences.t: τὸν βάλ’ ὑπὸ γναθμοῖο. καὶ οὔατος·
sentences.tr: ton bal’ hypo gnathmoio. kai ouatos·
sentences.l: Him he struck beneath the jaw and the ear;
sentences.i: Paris hit him beneath the jaw and the ear;
sentences.n: τόν is Euchenor, and the unnamed archer is Paris. βάλ’ is βάλε, the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘hit’. The edition puts a stop after γναθμοῖο ‘jaw’ (γναθμός), and καὶ οὔατος then adds ‘and ear’ to the same ὑπό: the genitive οὔατος is the epic form of οὖς ‘ear’. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὦκα δὲ θυμὸς
ᾤχετ’ ἀπὸ μελέων, στυγερὸς δ’ ἄρα μιν σκότος εἷλεν.
sentences.tr:
ōka de thymos
ōichet’ apo meleōn, stygeros d’ ara min skotos heilen.
sentences.l:
and quickly the spirit
went from his limbs, and hateful darkness then seized him.
sentences.i: Quickly his spirit left his limbs, and hateful darkness seized him.
sentences.n: A death in the usual terms: the θυμός, the spirit that animates a man, leaves his limbs, and darkness takes him (compare the formula ‘darkness covered his eyes’, 4.461). ᾤχετ’ is ᾤχετο, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’, with the augment run into the root; μελέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of μέλος ‘limb’. ἄρα marks the outcome as natural, ‘then’. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν μάρναντο δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men marnanto demas pyros aithomenoio·
sentences.l: So they, for their part, fought in the likeness of blazing fire;
sentences.i: So they fought, like a blazing fire;
sentences.n: ὣς closes the account of Euchenor and turns to the general fighting; οἳ μέν ‘they, for their part’ waits for the δέ of Ἕκτωρ δ’ in the next line. μάρναντο is the imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’; δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο is ‘in the likeness of blazing fire’, with δέμας ‘body, form’ as an adverbial accusative and αἰθομένοιο the participle of αἴθω ‘burn’. The same line stands at 11.596.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ οὐκ ἐπέπυστο Διῒ φίλος, οὐδέ τι ᾔδη
ὅττί ῥά οἱ νηῶν ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ δηϊόωντο
λαοὶ ὑπ’ Ἀργείων.
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ ouk epepysto Diï philos, oude ti ēidē
hotti rha hoi nēōn ep’ aristera dēïoōnto
laoi hyp’ Argeiōn.
sentences.l:
But Hector, dear to Zeus, had not learned, nor did he know at all
that for him on the left of the ships were being cut down
the people by the Argives.
sentences.i: But Hector, dear to Zeus, had not learned of it and did not know at all that on the left of the ships his troops were being cut down by the Argives.
sentences.n: ἐπέπυστο is the pluperfect of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn’, used as a simple past, and ᾔδη the epic pluperfect of οἶδα ‘he knew’ (Attic ᾔδει). ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’ with the metrical doubling. οἱ is a dative of interest, ‘for him’, which marks the λαοί as his own side, and δηϊόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect passive of δηϊόω ‘cut down’. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
τάχα δ’ ἂν καὶ κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
ἔπλετο· τοῖος γὰρ γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος
ὄτρυν’ Ἀργείους, πρὸς δὲ σθένει αὐτὸς ἄμυνεν·
sentences.tr:
tacha d’ an kai kydos Achaiōn
epleto· toios gar gaiēochos ennosigaios
otryn’ Argeious, pros de sthenei autos amynen·
sentences.i: and soon the glory would even have been the Achaeans’; for one such as the earth-holder, the earth-shaker, was urging on the Argives, and he himself added his strength to their defence;
sentences.n: τάχα … ἂν … ἔπλετο is ‘would soon have been’: ἄν with a past tense (ἔπλετο, ‘came to be’) says what was near to happening. The god is Poseidon, who has been urging the Argives on since 13.43, but the Greek does not name him and neither layer supplies the name (γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος, ‘earth-holder, earth-shaker’). τοῖος is ‘of such a sort’ and looks back to the situation. ὄτρυν’ is the unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’; πρός is an adverb ‘besides’, σθένει ‘with might’, and ἄμυνεν has no object. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔχεν ᾗ τὰ πρῶτα πύλας καὶ τεῖχος ἐσᾶλτο
ῥηξάμενος Δαναῶν πυκινὰς στίχας ἀσπιστάων,
ἔνθ’ ἔσαν Αἴαντός τε νέες καὶ Πρωτεσιλάου
θῖν’ ἔφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς εἰρυμέναι·
sentences.tr:
all’ echen hēi ta prōta pylas kai teichos esalto
rhēxamenos Danaōn pykinas stichas aspistaōn,
enth’ esan Aiantos te nees kai Prōtesilaou
thin’ eph’ halos poliēs eirymenai·
sentences.l:
but he held on, where first he leapt in at the gates and the wall,
having broken the solid ranks of the Danaan shield-bearers,
where were the ships of Ajax and of Protesilaus
on the shore of the grey sea drawn up;
sentences.i: but he held on at the place where he had first leapt in at the gates and the wall, having broken the solid ranks of the Danaan shield-bearers, where the ships of Ajax and Protesilaus stood drawn up on the shore of the grey sea;
sentences.n: The subject is still Hector. ἔχεν has no object (‘held on’), and ᾗ τὰ πρῶτα ‘where at first’ points back to his leap at the gate (12.466). ἐσᾶλτο is the aorist of ἐσάλλομαι ‘leap in at’, with the places in the accusative, and ῥηξάμενος the aorist middle participle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. ἀσπιστάων is the epic genitive plural of ἀσπιστής ‘shield-bearer’, πυκινάς the house ‘solid’. Αἴαντος has no patronymic here, νέες is the epic nominative plural of ναῦς, and θῖν’ is θῖνα ‘shore’ after ἔφ’ (ἐπί). εἰρυμέναι is the perfect passive participle of ἐρύω ‘draw up’. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὕπερθε
τεῖχος ἐδέδμητο χθαμαλώτατον, ἔνθα μάλιστα
ζαχρηεῖς γίγνοντο μάχῃ αὐτοί τε καὶ ἵπποι.
sentences.tr:
autar hyperthe
teichos ededmēto chthamalōtaton, entha malista
zachrēeis gignonto machēi autoi te kai hippoi.
sentences.l:
but above them
the wall had been built lowest, where most of all
very violent became in the fight both the men themselves and the horses.
sentences.i: but above them the wall had been built lowest, and there, above all, both men and horses grew very violent in the fight.
sentences.n: The wall is lowest where Hector broke in, and the fighting is fiercest there (ἔνθα μάλιστα ‘where most of all’). ὕπερθε is ‘above’. ἐδέδμητο is the pluperfect passive of δέμω ‘build’, and χθαμαλώτατον the superlative of χθαμαλός ‘low, near the ground’. ζαχρηής is a rare word whose second half is not known; ζα- is the intensive ‘very’, and the translation is ‘very violent’. αὐτοί ‘the men themselves’ is set against ἵπποι ‘horses’. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ Βοιωτοὶ καὶ Ἰάονες ἑλκεχίτωνες
Λοκροὶ καὶ Φθῖοι καὶ φαιδιμόεντες Ἐπειοὶ
σπουδῇ ἐπαΐσσοντα νεῶν ἔχον, οὐδὲ δύναντο
ὦσαι ἀπὸ σφείων φλογὶ εἴκελον Ἕκτορα δῖον
οἳ μὲν Ἀθηναίων προλελεγμένοι·
sentences.tr:
entha de Boiōtoi kai Iaones helkechitōnes
Lokroi kai Phthioi kai phaidimoentes Epeioi
spoudēi epaïssonta neōn echon, oude dynanto
ōsai apo spheiōn phlogi eikelon Hektora dion
hoi men Athēnaiōn prolelegmenoi·
sentences.i: There the Boeotians and the Ionians with trailing tunics, the Locrians and Phthians and the shining Epeans, with effort held Hector back from the ships as he rushed on, but could not thrust heavenly Hector away from themselves, flame-like as he was; these were picked men of the Athenians;
sentences.n: Five peoples hold the line against Hector. ἑλκεχίτωνες, from ἕλκω ‘drag’ and χιτών ‘tunic’, is ‘with trailing tunics’, and φαιδιμόεντες is a stock epithet, ‘shining’, whose exact force is not known. σπουδῇ ‘with effort’ may go with ἔχον or with ἐπαΐσσοντα ‘rushing on’; the object Ἕκτορα waits until 688, and ἔχον with the genitive νεῶν is ‘kept him off the ships’. σφείων is the epic ‘themselves’ (genitive plural). οἳ μέν picks up the Ionians, who are the Athenians: προλελεγμένοι is the perfect passive participle of προλέγω ‘pick out’. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄρα τοῖσιν
ἦρχ’ υἱὸς Πετεῶο Μενεσθεύς, οἳ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
Φείδας τε Στιχίος τε Βίας τ’ ἐΰς·
sentences.tr:
en d’ ara toisin
ērch’ huios Peteōo Menestheus, hoi d’ ham’ heponto
Pheidas te Stichios te Bias t’ eÿs·
sentences.i: Menestheus, the son of Peteos, led them, and along with him followed Pheidas, Stichius and good Bias;
sentences.n: Menestheus is the Athenian leader (2.552), and Stichius is named with him as a commander of the Athenians at 13.195–196. ἦρχ’ is ἦρχε, the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead’. οἳ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο is ‘and along with him followed’, and the three names are the subject: Φείδας, Στιχίος and Βίας, who gets the epithet ἐΰς ‘good’. ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The unit begins and ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἐπειῶν
Φυλεΐδης τε Μέγης Ἀμφίων τε Δρακίος τε,
πρὸ Φθίων δὲ Μέδων τε μενεπτόλεμός τε Ποδάρκης.
sentences.tr:
autar Epeiōn
Phyleïdēs te Megēs Amphiōn te Drakios te,
pro Phthiōn de Medōn te meneptolemos te Podarkēs.
sentences.l:
and of the Epeans
Phyleus’-son Meges, and Amphion, and Dracius,
and before the Phthians Medon and steadfast-in-battle Podarces.
sentences.i: Of the Epeans the leaders were Meges, son of Phyleus, Amphion and Dracius, and at the head of the Phthians stood Medon and Podarces, steadfast in battle.
sentences.n: There is no verb: ἦρχ’ ‘led’ from the last unit is understood, so Meges, Amphion and Dracius are the Epean leaders, and Medon and Podarces stand ‘before’ the Phthians (πρό ‘in front of’, at their head). Φυλεΐδης is the patronymic ‘Phyleus’-son’; Meges is already a leader in the Catalogue (2.627). μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’ belongs to Ποδάρκης alone. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν νόθος υἱὸς Ὀϊλῆος θείοιο
ἔσκε Μέδων Αἴαντος ἀδελφεός·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ho men nothos huios Oïlēos theioio
eske Medōn Aiantos adelpheos·
sentences.l:
Now he, for his part, bastard son of divine Oileus,
was Medon, brother of Ajax;
sentences.i: Medon, for his part, was an illegitimate son of divine Oileus, and a brother of Ajax;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μέν ‘as for him’ is Medon, and αὐτὰρ ὃ in 698 answers it with Podarces. νόθος is ‘illegitimate’, born outside marriage, the description given of Medon in the Catalogue (2.727). ἔσκε is a form of εἰμί (= ἦν) with the -σκ- suffix, here with no iterative force, and ἀδελφεός is the epic ἀδελφός ‘brother’. Αἴαντος is the Ajax who is Oileus’ son, the one named by his father at 701. θείοιο ‘divine’ is Oileus’ epithet, kept as written. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔναιεν
ἐν Φυλάκῃ γαίης ἄπο πατρίδος ἄνδρα κατακτὰς
γνωτὸν μητρυιῆς Ἐριώπιδος, ἣν ἔχ’ Ὀϊλεύς·
sentences.tr:
autar enaien
en Phylakēi gaiēs apo patridos andra kataktas
gnōton mētruiēs Eriōpidos, hēn ech’ Oïleus·
sentences.i: but he lived in Phylace, away from his fatherland, after killing a man, a kinsman of his stepmother Eriopis, whom Oileus had as his wife;
sentences.n: The subject is Medon again, and the passage explains why he lives away from home. ἔναιεν is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’, and γαίης ἄπο πατρίδος has its preposition after the noun (ἀπό, accent drawn back), ‘away from his fatherland’. κατακτάς is the second aorist participle of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, in its short stem κτα- (Attic κατακτανών). γνωτόν ‘kinsman’ stands in apposition to ἄνδρα. μητρυιῆς is ‘stepmother’, Oileus’ wife; ἔχ’ is ἔχε ‘had’, of a wife. The line does not say why the killing mattered. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ Ἰφίκλοιο πάϊς τοῦ Φυλακίδαο.
sentences.tr: autar ho Iphikloio païs tou Phylakidao.
sentences.l: but the other, son of Iphiclus, that Phylacus’-son.
sentences.i: while the other, Podarces, was the son of Iphiclus, the son of Phylacus.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but the other’ answers ἤτοι ὃ μέν (694) and turns to Podarces. Ἰφίκλοιο is the epic genitive of Ἴφικλος, and πάϊς is the epic ‘son’ (= παῖς). Φυλακίδαο is the patronymic of Φύλακος, so the line says ‘Iphiclus, the son of Phylacus’; the Catalogue gives Podarces’ descent the same way (2.705). τοῦ is the article used as a pointing pronoun, ‘that’.

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν πρὸ Φθίων μεγαθύμων θωρηχθέντες
ναῦφιν ἀμυνόμενοι μετὰ Βοιωτῶν ἐμάχοντο·
sentences.tr:
hoi men pro Phthiōn megathymōn thōrēchthentes
nauphin amynomenoi meta Boiōtōn emachonto·
sentences.l:
These, in front of the great-hearted Phthians, having armed themselves,
warding off from the ships, fought among the Boeotians;
sentences.i: These, armed at the head of the great-hearted Phthians, fought among the Boeotians in defence of the ships;
sentences.n: οἳ μέν are the leaders just named, with their men, and the contrast comes in Αἴας δ’ at 701. θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm with a breastplate’, in the sense ‘armed themselves’. ναῦφιν has the old ending -φιν, here meaning ‘from’: ἀμυνόμενοι ναῦφιν is ‘warding off (the enemy) from the ships’. μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’ is kept as the house rendering; ἐμάχοντο is the imperfect of μάχομαι.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ οὐκέτι πάμπαν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς υἱὸς
ἵστατ’ ἀπ’ Αἴαντος Τελαμωνίου οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν,
ἀλλ’ ὥς τ’ ἐν νειῷ βόε οἴνοπε πηκτὸν ἄροτρον
ἶσον θυμὸν ἔχοντε τιταίνετον·
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ ouketi pampan Oïlēos tachys huios
histat’ ap’ Aiantos Telamōniou oud’ ēbaion,
all’ hōs t’ en neiōi boe oinope pēkton arotron
ison thymon echonte titaineton·
sentences.l:
But no longer at all did Ajax, swift son of Oileus,
stand apart from Telamonian Ajax, not even a little,
but as in fallow land two wine-faced oxen the jointed plough
with equal spirit draw;
sentences.i: But Ajax, the swift son of Oileus, no longer stood apart from Telamonian Ajax at all, not even a little; but, as two oxen with the look of wine draw the jointed plough in fallow land with equal spirit,
sentences.n: The two Ajaxes stand side by side, and a simile compares them to a pair of oxen. οὐκέτι πάμπαν ‘no longer at all’ and οὐδ’ ἠβαιόν ‘not even a little’ pile up the negatives. ἵστατ’ is ἵστατο, the imperfect middle of ἵστημι. βόε, οἴνοπε, ἔχοντε and τιταίνετον are duals, the Greek number for a pair. οἴνοπε is ‘wine-faced’ (the colour of the oxen is not more closely known), νειός ‘fallow land’, πηκτόν ‘fixed together, jointed’, ἄροτρον ‘plough’; the words βόε οἴνοπε πηκτὸν ἄροτρον stand in a simile at Odyssey 13.32. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρά σφι
πρυμνοῖσιν κεράεσσι πολὺς ἀνακηκίει ἱδρώς·
τὼ μέν τε ζυγὸν οἶον ἐΰξοον ἀμφὶς ἐέργει
ἱεμένω κατὰ ὦλκα· τέμει δέ τε τέλσον ἀρούρης·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ara sphi
prymnoisin keraessi polys anakēkiei hidrōs·
tō men te zygon oion eÿxoon amphis eergei
hiemenō kata ōlka· temei de te telson arourēs·
sentences.i: and around the roots of their horns much sweat wells up; only the well-polished yoke keeps the two apart as they press on along the furrow, and the plough cuts on to the field’s boundary;
sentences.n: The simile goes on with the oxen’s labour. ἀνακηκίει is ‘wells up’; σφι ‘their’ is a dative of interest, and πρυμνοῖσιν κεράεσσι the epic dative plural, ‘at the base of the horns’. ζυγόν is the yoke, ἐΰξοον ‘well-polished’ (the house word), and ἀμφὶς ἐέργει ‘holds apart’ (ἐέργω = εἴργω). ἱεμένω is a dual participle of ἵεμαι ‘press on’, and ὦλκα (ὦλξ) is ‘furrow’. τέμει is singular, so its subject is the plough of 703, not the pair; τέλσον ἀρούρης is ‘the boundary of the field’. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: ὣς τὼ παρβεβαῶτε μάλ’ ἕστασαν ἀλλήλοιιν.
sentences.tr: hōs tō parbebaōte mal’ hestasan allēloiin.
sentences.l: So the two, having stepped alongside, stood very close to one another.
sentences.i: So the two of them stood close beside each other.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile and brings the two Ajaxes back. τώ and the participle παρβεβαῶτε (the perfect of παραβαίνω, literally ‘having stepped alongside’) are duals, and ἕστασαν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, with a plural verb after a dual subject. ἀλλήλοιιν is the dual dative of ἀλλήλων ‘each other’. μάλ’ strengthens the nearness, ‘very close’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι Τελαμωνιάδῃ πολλοί τε καὶ ἐσθλοὶ
λαοὶ ἕπονθ’ ἕταροι, οἵ οἱ σάκος ἐξεδέχοντο
ὁππότε μιν κάματός τε καὶ ἱδρὼς γούναθ’ ἵκοιτο.
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi Telamōniadēi polloi te kai esthloi
laoi heponth’ hetaroi, hoi hoi sakos exedechonto
hoppote min kamatos te kai hidrōs gounath’ hikoito.
sentences.l:
But to Telamon’s-son many and good
people followed, companions, who his shield took over
whenever weariness and sweat should come upon him at the knees.
sentences.i: But many good troops followed the son of Telamon, his companions, who would take his shield from him whenever weariness and sweat came upon his knees.
sentences.n: Telamonian Ajax has companions to relieve him; the Locrians of the next line have none for the other Ajax. ἕπονθ’ is ἕποντο, with the τ aspirated before the rough breathing of ἕταροι. Τελαμωνιάδῃ is the dative of the patronymic, ‘Telamon’s-son’. ἐξεδέχοντο (ἐκδέχομαι ‘take over from’) with ὁππότε and the optative ἵκοιτο says what regularly happened, ‘would take’. κάματος ‘weariness’ and ἱδρώς ‘sweat’ are the compound subject of ἵκοιτο, and μιν … γούναθ’ (γούνατα) puts the person and the part, ‘him, at the knees’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ Ὀϊλιάδῃ μεγαλήτορι Λοκροὶ ἕποντο·
οὐ γάρ σφι σταδίῃ ὑσμίνῃ μίμνε φίλον κῆρ·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ar’ Oïliadēi megalētori Lokroi heponto·
ou gar sphi stadiēi hysminēi mimne philon kēr·
sentences.l:
But not with Oileus’-son, great-spirited, did the Locrians follow;
for not for them in the standing battle did the dear heart stay;
sentences.i: But the Locrians did not follow the great-spirited son of Oileus, for their heart did not hold firm in the battle where men stand their ground;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ‘but not’ sets the Locrians against the companions of 710. Ὀϊλιάδῃ is the dative of the patronymic, ‘Oileus’-son’, the lesser Ajax, and μεγαλήτορι ‘great-spirited’ is the house epithet. μίμνε is the unaugmented imperfect of μίμνω (= μένω) ‘stay, hold firm’; σφι ‘for them’ is a dative of interest. σταδίῃ ὑσμίνῃ is the ‘standing battle’ of hand-to-hand fighting, in which men hold their ground, and here the dative stands without ἐν.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔχον κόρυθας χαλκήρεας ἱπποδασείας,
οὐδ’ ἔχον ἀσπίδας εὐκύκλους καὶ μείλινα δοῦρα,
sentences.tr:
ou gar echon korythas chalkēreas hippodaseias,
oud’ echon aspidas eukyklous kai meilina doura,
sentences.l:
for they did not have helmets, bronze-fitted, horse-haired,
nor did they have shields, well-rounded, and ashen spears,
sentences.i: for they had neither bronze-fitted helmets thick with horsehair nor well-rounded shields and ashen spears,
sentences.n: What the Locrians lack, which the next unit completes. ἔχον is the imperfect of ἔχω ‘have’, with the negative twice (οὐ … οὐδ’). κόρυθας is the accusative plural of κόρυς ‘helmet’; χαλκήρεας ‘fitted with bronze’ and ἱπποδασείας ‘thick with horsehair’ (a crest of horsehair, ἵππος + δασύς ‘thick’) are stock epithets of helmets. εὐκύκλους ‘well-rounded’ goes with shields, and μείλινα ‘of ash’ (μελίη ‘ash-tree’) with spears. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence runs on a long way.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄρα τόξοισιν καὶ ἐϋστρεφεῖ οἶος ἀώτῳ
Ἴλιον εἰς ἅμ’ ἕποντο πεποιθότες, οἷσιν ἔπειτα
ταρφέα βάλλοντες Τρώων ῥήγνυντο φάλαγγας·
sentences.tr:
all’ ara toxoisin kai eÿstrephei oios aōtōi
Ilion eis ham’ heponto pepoithotes, hoisin epeita
tarphea ballontes Trōōn rhēgnynto phalangas·
sentences.i: but they came along to Ilios trusting in bows and in well-twisted sheep’s wool, and with these, then, shooting again and again, they broke the battle-lines of the Trojans;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄρα turns from what they lacked to what they had: bows, and a sling of twisted wool (compare 13.599–600, where a sling is made of well-twisted sheep’s wool). The edition prints οἶος here, which as a word would mean ‘alone’; the sense needed is οἰός ‘of a sheep’, as printed at 13.599 (οἰὸς ἀώτῳ), and the translation follows the sense. ἄωτος is ‘wool, a tuft of wool’. ἕποντο is ‘followed’, πεποιθότες ‘trusting’ (perfect participle of πείθομαι). ταρφέα is ‘often’ in the literal layer and ‘again and again’ in the free one (the house rendering), and ῥήγνυντο is the imperfect middle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’. The unit begins mid-way through a sentence.

sentences.t:
δή ῥα τόθ’ οἳ μὲν πρόσθε σὺν ἔντεσι δαιδαλέοισι
μάρναντο Τρωσίν τε καὶ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ,
οἳ δ’ ὄπιθεν βάλλοντες ἐλάνθανον· οὐδέ τι χάρμης
Τρῶες μιμνήσκοντο· συνεκλόνεον γὰρ ὀϊστοί.
sentences.tr:
dē rha toth’ hoi men prosthe syn entesi daidaleoisi
marnanto Trōsin te kai Hektori chalkokorystēi,
hoi d’ opithen ballontes elanthanon· oude ti charmēs
Trōes mimnēskonto· synekloneon gar oïstoi.
sentences.l:
So then those in front, with their wrought gear,
fought with the Trojans and with Hector, bronze-armed,
and those behind, casting, escaped notice; nor at all of the joy of battle
were the Trojans mindful; for the arrows threw them into confusion.
sentences.i: Then those in front, in their finely wrought gear, fought the Trojans and Hector, armed in bronze, while those behind shot without being noticed; and the Trojans did not remember the joy of battle at all, for the arrows threw them into confusion.
sentences.n: οἳ μέν … οἳ δέ divides the fighters: the men in front, in full armour, and the archers behind them, who are the Locrians of the last two units. ἔντεσι is the epic dative plural of ἔντεα ‘gear’, and δαιδαλέοισι ‘wrought’; χαλκοκορυστῇ is Hector’s epithet, ‘armed in bronze’ (κορύσσω ‘arm’). ἐλάνθανον is the imperfect of λανθάνω ‘escape notice’, with the participle βάλλοντες: they shot unseen. χάρμη is the ‘joy of battle’, μιμνήσκοντο the imperfect middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’ with the genitive, and συνεκλόνεον (συγκλονέω) ‘threw into confusion’, a rare verb.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κε λευγαλέως νηῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων
Τρῶες ἐχώρησαν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν,
εἰ μὴ Πουλυδάμας θρασὺν Ἕκτορα εἶπε παραστάς·
sentences.tr:
entha ke leugaleōs nēōn apo kai klisiaōn
Trōes echōrēsan proti Ilion ēnemoessan,
ei mē Poulydamas thrasyn Hektora eipe parastas·
sentences.l:
There, pitiably, from the ships and the huts
the Trojans would have gone back to windy Ilios,
had not Polydamas spoken to bold Hector, standing beside him:
sentences.i: Then the Trojans would have gone back, pitiably, from the ships and the huts to windy Ilios, had not Polydamas stood beside bold Hector and spoken:
sentences.n: ἔνθά κε … ἐχώρησαν ‘there they would have gone back’: κε with a past tense (the aorist ἐχώρησαν) says what would have happened, and εἰ μή ‘if not’ gives the condition, the usual way Homer shows a danger just avoided. λευγαλέως is ‘pitiably’ (λευγαλέος ‘pitiful’). ἄπο follows its noun, νηῶν ἄπο = ἀπὸ νηῶν, and κλισιάων is the epic genitive plural of κλισία ‘hut’. Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν ‘windy Ilios’ and θρασύς ‘bold’ are stock epithets. εἶπε παραστάς ‘spoke, standing beside’ introduces the speech.

sentences.t: Ἕκτορ ἀμήχανός ἐσσι παραρρητοῖσι πιθέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Hektor amēchanos essi pararrētoisi pithesthai.
sentences.l: “Hector, past all dealing with you are, to yield to words of persuasion.
sentences.i: “Hector, you are impossible to deal with when it comes to yielding to persuasion.
sentences.n: Polydamas begins bluntly. ἀμήχανος literally ‘without resource’ is said of how Hector is to be handled: nothing can be done with him by persuasion, and the translation is the one given to ἀμήχανος said of Nestor at 10.167. ἐσσι is the epic ‘you are’ (= εἶ). παραρρητοῖσι is the dative of παράρρητος, ‘words that win a man over’ (from παρά and ἐρέω ‘speak’), after πιθέσθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of πείθω, ‘to be persuaded by’. The speech runs to line 747.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκά τοι περὶ δῶκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα
τοὔνεκα καὶ βουλῇ ἐθέλεις περιίδμεναι ἄλλων·
sentences.tr:
houneka toi peri dōke theos polemēïa erga
touneka kai boulēi etheleis periidmenai allōn·
sentences.l:
Because to you above others a god has given the works of war,
for that reason you wish also in counsel to know beyond others;
sentences.i: Because a god has given you the deeds of war beyond others, you therefore want to know more than others in counsel too;
sentences.n: οὕνεκα … τοὔνεκα ‘because … for that reason’ makes Hector’s gift the ground of his claim; τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα. τοι is the enclitic σοι ‘to you’. περὶ δῶκε: περί is an adverb ‘beyond (others)’, and δῶκε the aorist of δίδωμι. θεός without an article is ‘a god’. πολεμήϊα ἔργα is ‘the works of war’. περιίδμεναι is the epic infinitive of περίοιδα ‘know beyond’, with the genitive ἄλλων of comparison, ‘more than others’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ἅμα πάντα δυνήσεαι αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.tr: all’ ou pōs hama panta dynēseai autos helesthai.
sentences.l: But in no way all things at once will you be able yourself to take.
sentences.i: But you will not be able to take everything for yourself at once.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ‘but in no way’ turns against the claim just made. δυνήσεαι is the epic uncontracted future of δύναμαι (Attic δυνήσῃ); αὐτός ‘yourself’ stresses the single man; ἑλέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of αἱρέω, ‘to take for oneself’. The same thought, that the gods do not give men everything at once, is put at 4.320 (ἅμα πάντα).

sentences.t:
ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα,
ἄλλῳ δ’ ὀρχηστύν, ἑτέρῳ κίθαριν καὶ ἀοιδήν,
sentences.tr:
allōi men gar edōke theos polemēïa erga,
allōi d’ orchēstyn, heterōi kitharin kai aoidēn,
sentences.l:
For to one a god has given the works of war,
to another dancing, to another the lyre and song,
sentences.i: For to one man a god has given the deeds of war, to another dancing, and to another the lyre and song,
sentences.n: A general truth in a list: ἄλλῳ μέν … ἄλλῳ δ’ … ἑτέρῳ ‘to one … to another … to another’, where ἄλλῳ and ἑτέρῳ mean the same. ἔδωκε is the aorist used of what happens in general, and the English perfect keeps it as a standing fact. ὀρχηστύς ‘dancing’ (accusative ὀρχηστύν), κίθαρις ‘lyre’ (accusative κίθαριν) and ἀοιδή ‘song’ are gifts that are not war; θεός is again ‘a god’, and the next line names Zeus. The unit ends at a comma, since the sentence continues.

sentences.t:
ἄλλῳ δ’ ἐν στήθεσσι τιθεῖ νόον εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἐσθλόν, τοῦ δέ τε πολλοὶ ἐπαυρίσκοντ’ ἄνθρωποι,
καί τε πολέας ἐσάωσε, μάλιστα δὲ καὐτὸς ἀνέγνω.
sentences.tr:
allōi d’ en stēthessi tithei noon euryopa Zeus
esthlon, tou de te polloi epauriskont’ anthrōpoi,
kai te poleas esaōse, malista de kautos anegnō.
sentences.l:
and to another in his breast puts a mind, far-thundering Zeus,
good, of him many men have the benefit,
and he has saved many, and most of all he himself has recognised it.
sentences.i: To another, far-thundering Zeus puts a good mind in his breast; many men have the benefit of him, and he has saved many, and most of all he himself has recognised it.
sentences.n: τιθεῖ is the epic third singular of τίθημι (= τίθησι), a present that states a general truth. εὐρύοπα ‘far-thundering’ is the traditional reading of an epithet whose second part is disputed. τοῦ can be read ‘of him’ or ‘of it’ (the man or the mind); the translation takes ‘him’, since the verbs after it (ἐσάωσε, ἀνέγνω) have the man as subject. ἐπαυρίσκοντ’ is ἐπαυρίσκονται ‘have the benefit’, with the genitive. ἐσάωσε is the aorist of σαόω ‘save’, and ἀνέγνω ‘recognised’ has no object in the Greek, so ‘it’ is supplied. καὐτός is καὶ αὐτός.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα·
sentences.tr: autar egōn ereō hōs moi dokei einai arista·
sentences.l: But I shall say as it seems to me to be best.
sentences.i: But I will say it as it seems best to me.
sentences.n: Polydamas turns from the general truth to his own advice. ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ, and ἐρέω the uncontracted future of ἐρῶ ‘I shall say’. ὥς μοι δοκεῖ εἶναι ἄριστα is ‘as it seems to me to be best’, with ἄριστα the neuter plural used as a superlative. The line is the same as Nestor’s at 9.103.

sentences.t: πάντῃ γάρ σε περὶ στέφανος πολέμοιο δέδηε·
sentences.tr: pantēi gar se peri stephanos polemoio dedēe·
sentences.l: for on every side around you a crown of war is blazing;
sentences.i: for a ring of war is blazing all about you;
sentences.n: πάντῃ ‘on every side’ and σε περί (the preposition set after its pronoun, = περί σε) place Hector at the centre. στέφανος is a crown or wreath, here a ring; the image is a circle of fire. πολέμοιο ‘of war’ is the genitive of what the crown is made of. δέδηε is the perfect of δαίω ‘kindle’ in its intransitive sense, ‘is ablaze, burns’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ μεγάθυμοι ἐπεὶ κατὰ τεῖχος ἔβησαν
οἳ μὲν ἀφεστᾶσιν σὺν τεύχεσιν, οἳ δὲ μάχονται
παυρότεροι πλεόνεσσι κεδασθέντες κατὰ νῆας.
sentences.tr:
Trōes de megathymoi epei kata teichos ebēsan
hoi men aphestasin syn teuchesin, hoi de machontai
pauroteroi pleonessi kedasthentes kata nēas.
sentences.l:
and the Trojans, great-hearted, when along the wall they went,
some stand apart with their armour, and some fight,
fewer against more, scattered along the ships.
sentences.i: As for the great-hearted Trojans, now that they have crossed the wall, some of them stand aloof with their armour, while others fight, fewer against more, scattered along the ships.
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ κατὰ τεῖχος ἔβησαν is ‘when they went along (over) the wall’, that is, once they had crossed it. οἳ μέν … οἳ δέ divide the Trojans into those who hold back and those who fight. ἀφεστᾶσιν is the epic perfect of ἀφίστημι, ‘stand apart’, and τεύχεσιν the dative plural of τεῦχος ‘armour’ (τεύχεα in the plural). παυρότεροι ‘fewer’ is set against πλεόνεσσι ‘more’ (epic dative plural), and κεδασθέντες is the aorist passive participle of κεδάννυμι ‘scatter’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀναχασσάμενος κάλει ἐνθάδε πάντας ἀρίστους·
sentences.tr: all’ anachassamenos kalei enthade pantas aristous·
sentences.l: but drawing back, call here all the best;
sentences.i: but fall back, and call all the best men here;
sentences.n: ἀναχασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, and it carries the first order: pull back, then call. κάλει is the present imperative of καλέω (‘call!’), not an imperfect. ἐνθάδε is ‘here’; πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best’ are the chiefs, whom Hector is to bring to council.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δ’ ἂν μάλα πᾶσαν ἐπιφρασσαίμεθα βουλὴν
ἤ κεν ἐνὶ νήεσσι πολυκλήϊσι πέσωμεν
αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι θεὸς δόμεναι κράτος, ἦ κεν ἔπειτα
πὰρ νηῶν ἔλθωμεν ἀπήμονες.
sentences.tr:
enthen d’ an mala pasan epiphrassaimetha boulēn
ē ken eni nēessi polyklēïsi pesōmen
ai k’ ethelēisi theos domenai kratos, ē ken epeita
par nēōn elthōmen apēmones.
sentences.l:
From there we might well consider the whole plan,
whether among the many-thwarted ships we should fall,
if a god is willing to grant strength, or then
from beside the ships we should go, unharmed.
sentences.i: From there we could thoroughly consider the whole plan: whether to throw ourselves among the ships of many thwarts, if a god is willing to grant us strength, or else to go away from the ships unharmed.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν ‘from there’ looks forward to the council. ἂν … ἐπιφρασσαίμεθα is a potential optative, ‘we might consider’, and ἤ … ἦ gives the two alternatives (ἤ … ἦ both ‘whether … or’). πέσωμεν and ἔλθωμεν are aorist subjunctives in the question. αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσι is the epic εἰ ἐθέλῃ, ‘if he is willing’; δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι; κράτος ‘strength’ is here near ‘the upper hand’. πὰρ νηῶν is παρὰ νηῶν, ‘from beside the ships’, and ἀπήμονες ‘unharmed’. The unit ends mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ἔγωγε
δείδω μὴ τὸ χθιζὸν ἀποστήσωνται Ἀχαιοὶ
χρεῖος, ἐπεὶ παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀνὴρ ἆτος πολέμοιο
μίμνει, ὃν οὐκέτι πάγχυ μάχης σχήσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.tr:
ē gar egōge
deidō mē to chthizon apostēsōntai Achaioi
chreios, epei para nēusin anēr atos polemoio
mimnei, hon ouketi panchy machēs schēsesthai oïō.
sentences.l:
For truly I myself
fear lest yesterday’s debt the Achaeans
exact back, since beside the ships a man insatiate of war
stays, whom no longer wholly from battle will hold back, I think.”
sentences.i: For truly I fear that the Achaeans may exact their debt of yesterday, since beside the ships a man who never has enough of war remains, and I think he will no longer hold himself wholly aloof from the fighting.”
sentences.n: δείδω μή with the subjunctive ἀποστήσωνται is ‘I fear lest they …’, and ἀποστήσωνται χρεῖος (the middle of ἀφίστημι) is to exact payment of a debt; τὸ χθιζὸν χρεῖος is ‘yesterday’s debt’; the Greek does not spell out the debt, which is the reckoning the Achaeans are owed for the earlier fighting. The man at the ships (ἀνήρ ἆτος πολέμοιο, ‘insatiate of war’) is not named, and he is understood to be Achilles. ἆτος is the house ‘insatiate of war’. σχήσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of ἔχω, ‘hold oneself back’, with the genitive μάχης; ὀΐω is ‘I think’. The unit begins mid-line and closes the speech.
